findings.finding: 0% of trades were accepted even though the listener got it wrong; 10 of 48 words in use now started as a mistake (misheard, or coined for something else).
findings.evidence: Wrenford "ko" = two: misheard: ka → ko (generation 3) · Wrenford "thu" = yes: misheard: tho → thu (generation 7) · Oakhollow "thoga" = planks: misheard: thoka → thoga (generation 11)

findings.q: Do the words used most change least?
findings.finding: Use vs. replacement rate across meanings: ρ = -0.51, p = 0.090, n = 12. Most used: two (15% replaced per generation), wood (13% replaced per generation), food (19% replaced per generation); least: planks (17%), five (63%).
findings.evidence: Real languages show this (Pagel et al. 2007). n = meanings, so treat as suggestive.

findings.q: Do a few families take over, and does the language narrow with them?
findings.finding: By generation 19, every living agent descends from one founder. Families alive vs. distinct words per meaning across towns: ρ = 0.74, p = <0.001, n = 25.
findings.evidence: Children go to the best-placed parents, so lineages die out: a founder effect, as in population genetics. Caution: families and variety both fall over time, so the correlation may be the language converging, not the families narrowing it.
